title: The extended life cycle
blurb: Define the extended project life cycle and explain why it adds Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition.
question: A council's new repairs app was handed over in April and the project team has moved on. In October, the sponsor is still checking whether repair times have fallen as the business case promised. Which life cycle includes this work, and which phases does it add?

teach.h: The project doesn't stop at handover
teach.body: An extended life cycle is a linear life cycle extended with two extra phases after Transition: Adoption and Benefits realisation. The life cycle continues until the benefits promised in the business case are realised. In plain English: handing over a new system isn't the finish line. People have to start using it properly, and only then do the savings or improvements actually arrive.

teach.h: The six phases of the extended life cycle

steps.label: Adoption
steps.sub: Users take up the change in BAU

teach.caption: The first four are the linear life cycle. The last two are what make it 'extended'.

teach.h: Why extend it? Outputs are not benefits
teach.body: A project delivers outputs, such as a new app. A benefit is a measurable improvement from an outcome, perceived as an advantage by stakeholders, such as faster repairs. Most benefits only arrive after handover, once people have changed how they work. The extended life cycle keeps attention on the business case until those benefits are realised. The sponsor is accountable for benefits, and many are realised after the project team has closed.

steps.label: Adoption
steps.sub: Staff and tenants actually use it; the phone queue is retired

steps.label: Benefit
steps.sub: Repairs are completed faster, as the business case predicted

teach.h: What happens in the two extra phases
head: Phase
What happens
Example
rows: Users take up the new outputs and ways of working in BAU
Repair staff use the app; old phone line closed
Benefits are tracked and confirmed against the business case
Repair times measured and reported to the sponsor

teach.body: The app is built and handed over in April (Transition). Through the summer, staff are supported to use it, tenants are encouraged to report repairs online, and the old phone line is closed (Adoption). From autumn, the council measures repair times against the business case and reports to the sponsor (Benefits realisation). In a plain linear life cycle, the story would have ended in April, before any benefit had been proven.

items.label: Transition
items.sub: App handed over; project team released

items.label: Adoption
items.sub: Staff and tenants switch to the app

items.label: Benefits realisation
items.sub: Repair times tracked against the business case

teach.caption: Illustrative timings. Benefits usually arrive well after the outputs are handed over.

teach.text: Classic distractor: 'an approach that adds operational and termination phases'. That is NOT the extended project life cycle: it adds ADOPTION and BENEFITS REALISATION. It is also not 'a framework for a cost-benefit analysis after closure'. Older material may describe it as the linear phases 'plus benefits realisation'; for the PFQ, learn Adoption and Benefits realisation.

items: Extended life cycle: a linear life cycle plus Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition.
Order: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition, Adoption, Benefits realisation.
It continues until the benefits in the business case are realised.
Reason: benefits usually arrive after handover, once the change is adopted.
Not 'operations and termination', and not the same as hybrid.

summary: You can now define the extended project life cycle and list its six phases in order. You can also explain why Adoption and Benefits realisation follow Transition: benefits usually arrive only once the change is in use.

A.q: Which TWO phases does the extended life cycle add to a linear life cycle?
A.why: The extended life cycle adds Adoption and Benefits realisation after Transition.

whyNot.0: Operations and termination is a common distractor; it is not the extended project life cycle.
whyNot.1: Feasibility and Foundations are the first two iterative phases.
whyNot.3: Closure and the post-project review happen at the end of the linear phases; they are not the added phases.

A.q: In an extended life cycle, which phase immediately follows Transition?
A.why: After Transition comes Adoption, then Benefits realisation.

whyNot.2: Benefits realisation is the final phase, after Adoption.
whyNot.3: Closure happens within Transition; it isn't a separate extended phase.

A.q: What is the final phase of an extended project life cycle?
A.why: The extended life cycle ends with Benefits realisation, when the business case benefits are achieved.

whyNot.0: Transition is the last LINEAR phase; the extended life cycle carries on after it.
whyNot.2: A post-project review evaluates how the project was managed; it isn't a phase of the extended life cycle.

B.q: Why does an extended life cycle continue after Transition?
options: The outputs are not yet fully built
The team must repeat its time boxes
The business case is not yet written
B.why: Benefits usually arrive once the outputs are adopted in use, which is after handover. The extended life cycle runs until they are realised.

whyNot.1: Outputs are built in Deployment and handed over in Transition.
whyNot.2: Time boxes belong to iterative development, not to the extension.
whyNot.3: The business case is written early, in Concept and Definition.

B.q: Complete the sequence: Concept, Definition, Deployment, Transition, ___, Benefits realisation.
B.why: Adoption sits between Transition and Benefits realisation.

whyNot.0: 'Operation' is a distractor; the APM phase is Adoption.
whyNot.1: Closure takes place within Transition, not after it.
whyNot.2: Evaluation is an activity, not a phase name in this model.

B.q: Six months after handover, the sponsor checks whether repair times have fallen as the business case promised. Which phase is this?
B.why: Tracking and confirming benefits against the business case is Benefits realisation.

whyNot.0: Transition was the handover six months earlier.
whyNot.1: Handover and closure is older wording for the end of the linear phases, which finished six months earlier.
whyNot.3: Adoption is users taking up the change; here the sponsor is measuring the benefit.

C.q: Staff are being supported to use a new system day to day, and the old paper process is being withdrawn. Which extended phase is this?
C.why: Users taking up the new outputs and ways of working in business as usual is Adoption.

whyNot.0: Deployment builds and tests the outputs before handover.
whyNot.2: Transition hands the outputs over; embedding their use comes next.
whyNot.3: Benefits realisation measures the improvements once the change is adopted.

C.q: Which statement about the extended project life cycle is NOT correct?
options: It adds operational and termination phases
It runs until the benefits are realised
Its first four phases are the linear ones
C.why: The extended life cycle adds Adoption and Benefits realisation, not operational and termination phases.

whyNot.1: True: it continues until the business case benefits are realised.
whyNot.2: True: Concept, Definition, Deployment and Transition come first.
whyNot.3: True: users must adopt the change before benefits can be realised.

C.q: Who is accountable for the benefits tracked in the Benefits realisation phase?
C.why: The sponsor owns the business case and is accountable for benefits realisation, often long after the project team has closed.

whyNot.0: The project manager delivers the outputs; by this phase they have usually moved on.
whyNot.2: The team is released at Transition.
whyNot.3: End users adopt the change and so enable benefits, but they aren't accountable for them.

reteach.title: The gym membership
reteach.question: You buy a home gym to get fitter. Is the 'project' finished when the equipment is delivered and set up, or when you are actually fitter?

blocks.h: Delivered is not the same as done
blocks.body: Choosing, ordering and installing the gym is the linear part, ending at handover (Transition). But the reason you bought it was to get fitter. First you have to build the habit of using it (Adoption). Only months later can you check whether you are fitter (Benefits realisation). An extended life cycle simply keeps going until that real goal is met.

blocks.text: An unused gym delivers no benefit. That's why Adoption must come before Benefits realisation.

explain.body: An extended life cycle is a linear life cycle extended with Adoption and Benefits realisation phases, so the life cycle continues until the benefits promised in the business case are realised.

items.label: phases in the extended life cycle

test.q: Which of the following best defines an extended project life cycle?
options: A linear life cycle with phases added
A mix of linear and iterative working
An iterative life cycle with more sprints
A review of costs once a project closes
test.why: It is a linear life cycle with Adoption and Benefits realisation phases added after Transition.

whyNot.1: Mixing linear and iterative working is a hybrid life cycle.
whyNot.2: Extra sprints don't make a life cycle extended.
whyNot.3: A post-closure cost review is not the definition of the extended life cycle.

explain.body: After handover, users take up the new outputs and ways of working in business as usual. Old processes are withdrawn. Without adoption, no benefits can follow.

test.q: What mainly happens in the Adoption phase?
options: The outline business case is set
Users take up the change in BAU
Time boxes are planned and run
test.why: Adoption is when users take up the new outputs and ways of working in business as usual.

whyNot.1: The outline business case is produced in Concept.
whyNot.3: Time boxes belong to iterative development.

explain.body: The final phase. Benefits are tracked and confirmed against the business case, often long after the project team has gone. The sponsor is accountable for them.

test.q: In Benefits realisation, what are the benefits compared against?
test.why: Benefits are tracked and confirmed against those promised in the business case.

whyNot.0: Lessons learned capture how the project was managed, not the benefits it promised.
whyNot.2: The risk register records risks, not the benefits to be achieved.
whyNot.3: Time box plans belong to iterative development.

explain.body: A plain linear life cycle ends at Transition, when outputs are handed over. But benefits arrive later, once the change is adopted. Extending the life cycle keeps the focus on the reason the project was started.

test.q: A sponsor wants the life cycle to keep running until promised savings are proven. Which life cycle suits this?
test.why: Only the extended life cycle continues past Transition until the business case benefits are realised.

whyNot.0: Hybrid mixes approaches but doesn't, by definition, run on to benefits.
whyNot.1: Iterative delivers in time boxes; it isn't defined by running to benefits.
whyNot.2: A linear life cycle ends at Transition, before most benefits arrive.
